blogs.title: The Great Mimicker: When Uterine Fibroids Disguise as Adnexal Masses in Pregnancy
blogs.description: This post explores the diagnostic trap encountered when large pedunculated or cystic-degenerating leiomyomas mimic ovarian endometriomas during pregnancy. We dissect the specific imaging features that led the multidisciplinary team astray—including the inability to identify a connecting stalk or feeding vessel due to the 'steric bulk' of the gravid uterus—and discuss how the intraoperative finding of a twisted, leaking pedunculated fibroid fundamentally changed the surgical plan. The post emphasizes the importance of maintaining a broad differential diagnosis for cystic abdominal masses in pregnancy and highlights the limitations of preoperative imaging when anatomy is distorted by the enlarging uterus.

blogs.title: CA-125 in Pregnancy: A Tale of False Positives and Physiological Peaks
blogs.description: This post examines the interpretation of serum CA-125 during pregnancy, using the case's slightly elevated value of 41.8 U/mL as a springboard. We review the physiological peaks of CA-125 in the first and third trimesters, the normal range during the second trimester, and the myriad benign conditions that can elevate this marker—including endometriosis, adenomyosis, myomas, and pregnancy itself. The post critically evaluates how reliance on a single tumor marker nearly biased the team toward a diagnosis of decidualised endometrioma, and discusses the role of serial measurements and the danger of anchoring on oncologic markers in a pregnant population with low pretest probability of malignancy.

blogs.title: Scalpel vs. Patience: Surgical Decision-Making for Symptomatic Pelvic Masses in Pregnancy
blogs.description: This post analyzes the complex decision of when to operate on large symptomatic masses during pregnancy versus pursuing conservative management. We explore the specific indications that drove the team to proceed with surgery at 21+6 weeks—worsening pain, dyspnea from mass effect, risk of torsion/rupture/infection, and concerns about continued uterine enlargement—and contrast these with the general principle of delaying surgery until postpartum. The post also examines the rationale for removing only the cranial pedunculated myoma while leaving the caudal mass in situ, illustrating the principle of minimizing obstetric risk through targeted, pregnancy-preserving surgery. We discuss the laparotomy-versus-laparoscopy decision and the selection bias that favors open approaches for larger, multiple, or intramural masses.

blogs.title: Blind Spots: Navigating Imaging Limitations in the Gravid Abdomen
blogs.description: This post focuses on the imaging challenges unique to evaluating abdominal masses in pregnancy, where options are constrained by fetal safety. We discuss the complementary roles of ultrasound with color Doppler and non-contrast MRI, the specific reasons gadolinium is avoided, and the practical limitations encountered when a massive gravid uterus obscures vascular pedicles and anatomical relationships. The post also addresses the safety considerations of 1.5-T MRI after the first trimester and the clinical compromise inherent in accepting reduced diagnostic certainty to protect the fetus. We conclude with practical guidance on how to integrate imaging findings with clinical examination and tumor marker trends when definitive imaging characterization is impossible.

blogs.title: Protecting the Pregnancy: Tocolysis, Progesterone Prophylaxis, and Post-Myomectomy Care
blogs.description: This post examines the perioperative obstetric management strategies used to preserve pregnancy after myomectomy at 21+6 weeks, including intraoperative and postoperative progesterone prophylaxis (100 mg IM daily), continued hydroxyprogesterone caproate until delivery, serial fetal heart rate monitoring throughout surgery, and antibiotic selection guided by concurrent Klebsiella pneumoniae bacteriuria. We review the evidence—or lack thereof—behind these interventions and discuss the management of postoperative anemia (Hb drop to 7.5 g/dL requiring transfusion and IV iron), the 10-day hospitalization, and the subsequent strict obstetric follow-up every 3 weeks. The post critically evaluates which perioperative measures are evidence-based versus reflexive in this rare clinical scenario.

blogs.title: The Residual Mass: Planning Delivery and Postpartum Management of Persistent Fibroids
blogs.description: This post addresses the long-term obstetric decision-making following partial myomectomy in pregnancy, focusing on how the residual 9 cm caudal myoma influenced the planned mode and timing of delivery. We discuss the rationale for elective cesarean at 37 weeks via the same surgical scar, the concern that the pelvic mass would obstruct fetal head descent during labor, and the strategy of minimizing uterine scar rupture risk by using the previous incision. The post also reviews the natural history of leiomyomas in pregnancy—including the non-linear growth pattern, the significant postpartum regression (mean 44%), and the patient's decision to defer further surgery—and provides a framework for counseling patients about expected postpartum fibroid behavior and future reproductive planning.
